sessions.title: # Task: Configure the Complete Claude Code Agentic SDLC Framework Act as a Senior AI Agent Architect and Claude Code specialist. The repository structure already exists. Configure the complete Agentic SDLC framework using Claude Code's native capabilities. The objective is to create a reusable framework that can accept arbitrary application user stories and execute the software development lifecycle through specialized agents. Do not build an application as part of this task. --- ## 1. Architecture Follow the hybrid multi-agent architecture: - The main Claude Code session acts as the Orchestrator. - Eight specialized subagents handle individual SDLC responsibilities. - Skills define reusable workflows and slash commands. - Rules provide shared and path-specific instructions. - Hooks enforce important operational safeguards. - MCP integrations may provide external capabilities when configured. The Orchestrator must coordinate all agents and maintain workflow state. Specialist agents must not delegate to other specialist agents. Do not create a separate Orchestrator subagent. ## 2. Agent Definitions Create or improve the following files inside `.claude/agents/`: 1. `requirements-agent.md` 2. `architecture-agent.md` 3. `design-review-agent.md` 4. `planning-agent.md` 5. `implementation-agent.md` 6. `code-review-agent.md` 7. `verification-agent.md` 8. `pr-agent.md` Each agent must include: - Valid Claude Code subagent frontmatter. - Clear role and responsibilities. - Required input context. - Step-by-step execution process. - Expected deliverables. - Completion criteria. - Tool permissions following least privilege. - Restrictions and failure-handling rules. - Explicit handoff instructions to the Orchestrator. ### Agent responsibilities **Requirements Agent** - Analyze user stories and acceptance criteria. - Identify functional and non-functional requirements. - Detect ambiguities, missing information, and conflicts. - Ask clarification questions through the Orchestrator. - Create `docs/requirements.md`. **Architecture Agent** - Design the application architecture based on approved requirements. - Select the appropriate technology stack. - Document components, APIs, database design, data flow, and decisions. - Create `docs/architecture.md`. - Never assume a fixed language, framework, or database. **Design Review Agent** - Independently evaluate the architecture. - Identify design flaws, security concerns, scalability issues, and unnecessary complexity. - Create `docs/design-review.md`. - Never modify the architecture directly. **Planning Agent** - Convert approved architecture into actionable implementation tasks. - Identify dependencies, affected modules, and testing requirements. - Create `docs/impl-plan.md`. - Never start coding. **Implementation Agent** - Implement the approved application. - Follow the architecture and implementation plan. - Write appropriate automated tests. - Work exclusively on the `development` branch. - Report files changed and commands executed. **Code Review Agent** - Independently inspect implementation changes. - Identify bugs, security issues, code-quality problems, and requirement violations. - Classify findings by severity. - Create `docs/code-review.md`. - Must not modify application code. **Verification Agent** - Execute relevant tests and validation commands. - Verify implementation against acceptance criteria. - Create `docs/verification-report.md`. - Never fabricate test results. - Clearly distinguish executed, passed, failed, and skipped tests. **PR Agent** - Check workflow completion and approval status. - Prepare the pull request description. - Submit a PR from `development` to `main` only after explicit user approval. - Never merge the PR or bypass branch protection. ## 3. Skills Create reusable Claude Code skills under `.claude/skills/`. Each skill must have its own `SKILL.md` with valid Claude Code skill frontmatter, a clear purpose, execution instructions, expected inputs, outputs, and constraints. Create these skills: 1. `start-sdlc` - Main workflow entry point. - Coordinate the complete SDLC using the Orchestrator. - Resume from existing workflow state when appropriate. 2. `analyze-requirements` - Execute requirements analysis. - Identify missing information and clarification questions. 3. `design-architecture` - Produce architecture based on approved requirements. 4. `review-design` - Independently review architecture and report findings. 5. `create-implementation-plan` - Produce a detailed implementation plan. 6. `implement-feature` - Implement approved tasks on the development branch. 7. `review-code` - Perform independent code review. 8. `verify-application` - Execute tests and validate acceptance criteria. 9. `prepare-pr` - Validate completion and prepare or submit the pull request after approval. Skills must invoke or coordinate the appropriate specialist agents through the main session. Do not duplicate entire agent definitions inside skills. The `start-sdlc` skill should be usable as a slash command: `/start-sdlc` Do not create unnecessary skills or duplicate functionality. ## 4. Shared Instructions and Rules Create shared project instructions using `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/`. Create these rule files: - `general.md` - General project conventions. - Maintainability, readability, and simplicity. - `git-workflow.md` - Branching strategy. - Commit and pull request rules. - `security.md` - Secure coding practices. - Secrets management. - Input validation. - Sensitive information handling. - `testing.md` - Testing strategy. - Unit, integration, and relevant end-to-end testing. - Test evidence requirements. - `documentation.md` - Documentation standards. - Artifact naming and location. - Decision recording. - `agent-orchestration.md` - Orchestrator responsibilities. - Agent handoffs. - Workflow sequencing. - Approval gates. - Workflow-state management. Use path-specific rule frontmatter where it is useful and supported. Update `CLAUDE.md` to provide concise project-wide instructions and reference the shared rules. Avoid duplicating lengthy content already present in rule files. ## 5. Git Branching Strategy Enforce this two-branch strategy: ### main - Protected production branch. - No direct commits or pushes. - No agent can modify or merge into main. - Changes reach main only through an approved pull request. ### development - Main application development branch. - All implementation, bug fixes, and integration happen here. - No feature branches for the initial MVP. Before modifying files, the Implementation Agent must verify that the current branch is `development`. If the current branch is not `development`, stop and report the issue. Before any Git operation that changes repository state, inspect the working tree and preserve unrelated user changes. Never force-push, rewrite shared history, or bypass branch protection. ## 6. Hooks and Settings Configure `.claude/settings.json` and appropriate hook scripts under `.claude/hooks/`. Use hooks only for deterministic safeguards, such as: - Preventing accidental modifications to protected-branch workflows where feasible. - Detecting potentially unsafe operations. - Running lightweight validation when appropriate. - Enforcing basic project checks. Requirements: - Use valid Claude Code hook configuration and event names. - Keep hooks lightweight and understandable. - Do not use hooks as a substitute for agent reasoning or human approvals. - Do not introduce destructive automatic Git operations. - Do not execute commands without explaining their purpose. - Do not overwrite existing user settings. If a safeguard cannot reliably be enforced by a hook, document the limitation and enforce it through agent instructions. ## 7. Orchestration Workflow The main Claude Code session must coordinate these stages in order: 1. Requirements analysis. 2. Requirements clarification and user approval. 3. Architecture design. 4. Architecture approval. 5. Independent design review. 6. Implementation planning. 7. Implementation on `development`. 8. Independent code review. 9. Review-finding resolution and re-review. 10. Verification and testing. 11. Verification-failure resolution. 12. User approval before PR submission. 13. PR preparation and submission. The Orchestrator must maintain `docs/workflow-state.md`. Track: - Current stage. - Completed and pending stages. - Agent execution status. - Artifact locations. - Approval status. - Review findings. - Verification results. - Blockers. Important: - Explicitly pass relevant context and artifact paths between agents. - Do not assume subagents share conversation context. - Do not skip approval gates. - Do not silently change approved requirements. - Route review findings back to the responsible agent. - Resume from existing artifacts instead of repeating completed work unnecessarily. ## 8. Human Approval Gates Require explicit user approval: 1. Before finalizing requirements. 2. Before accepting the architecture. 3. Before submitting a PR. Never interpret silence as approval. Never allow an agent or skill to bypass these gates. ## 9. Generic Application Support The framework must work with arbitrary application requirements. Do not hardcode: - Expense Tracker functionality. - Programming languages. - Frameworks. - Databases. - Frontend or backend architectures. - Application-specific business rules. The Architecture Agent must select the appropriate stack based on the approved user story. Prefer the simplest solution that satisfies the requirements. ## 10. Documentation Update `README.md` with: - Framework overview. - Agent architecture. - Agent responsibilities. - Skills and slash commands. - Shared instruction structure. - Hook configuration. - Branching strategy. - How to start an SDLC workflow. - Approval gates. - How to provide a new user story. Keep the documentation practical and concise. ## 11. Scope Restrictions For this task: - Configure agents, skills, rules, hooks, and documentation. - Reuse existing project structure. - Inspect existing files before editing. - Preserve existing user changes. Do NOT: - Implement an application. - Generate application-specific source code. - Install unnecessary dependencies. - Create a separate orchestration backend. - Automatically connect external MCP servers. - Commit or push changes. - Modify remote branch protection settings. - Execute the SDLC workflow. ## 12. Final Validation After configuration: 1. Verify all eight agent files. 2. Verify all nine skills. 3. Verify all shared rule files. 4. Validate frontmatter and Claude Code conventions. 5. Validate hook configuration and referenced script paths. 6. Check for duplicate or conflicting instructions. 7. Verify agent permissions and handoff responsibilities. 8. Verify all approval gates. 9. Verify the development/main branching restrictions. 10. Verify the `/start-sdlc` skill entry point. 11. Show the final directory structure. 12. Summarize what was created and any limitations. Use Claude Code's supported native configuration conventions. Do not invent unsupported frontmatter fields, hook events, or configuration options. If a feature is unsupported or uncertain, explain the limitation instead of generating invalid configuration. Do not start application development.
